clinicalPearls: Cannabis is among the most widely used psychoactive substances; surveys cited estimate tens of millions of monthly users in the U.S., including a substantial number of adolescents and young adults aged 12-25.

Marijuana is legally distinguished from hemp by Delta-9-THC content: material exceeding 0.3% Delta-9-THC by dry weight is marijuana, while 0.3% or less is hemp; the principal euphoric and medicinal effects are mediated by Delta-9-THC acting on type 1 cannabinoid receptors (CB1R).

Product potency has risen sharply: flower can contain 20-30% Delta-9-THC, vape concentrates are advertised up to ~75%, and solid extracts ('shatter') up to ~95%, though many high claims appear exaggerated; higher potency is linked to greater addiction and psychosis risk.

Inhalation (smoking, vaping, 'dabbing') gives rapid, highly bioavailable absorption with quick onset, conditions associated with increased addiction risk; edibles have slower, less predictable onset and carry a higher risk of accidental overdose, particularly in children and inexperienced users.

Following smoking, plasma Delta-9-THC peaks within 5-10 minutes, but a hysteresis exists because brain levels keep rising during the early distribution (alpha) phase (t1/2 ~6 min) even as plasma falls; subjective peak effects occur at 20-30 minutes and total effect lasts roughly 4-8 hours.

Urine drug testing detects the inactive metabolite 11-nor-carboxy-THC (11-COOH-THC), whose terminal half-life is ~20 to 35+ hours, so cannabis remains detectable for days in occasional users and weeks in frequent users with saturated fat stores.

Regular use produces tolerance, so a given plasma Delta-9-THC level does not reliably predict impairment, which has hampered regulation of cannabis-impaired driving; Delta-9-THC nonetheless impairs judgment, motor coordination, and reaction time, increasing crash risk.

Cannabis use disorder (CUD) is a DSM-5 diagnosis defined by a problematic pattern of use causing clinically significant impairment or distress; criteria include craving, tolerance, a withdrawal syndrome, and failure to meet role obligations from recurrent use and drug seeking.

The withdrawal syndrome peaks within 1-3 days of stopping and manifests as anxiety, restlessness, insomnia, depression, and reduced appetite; most symptoms resolve within about 2 weeks, but insomnia often persists longer and may drive relapse.

Chronic high-dose use can cause cannabis hyperemesis syndrome, presenting as recurrent cycles of severe nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, and is a growing reason for ED visits and hospitalization.

High-potency cannabis (>10% THC) can trigger acute psychotic episodes even on first exposure; these are usually transient but may become chronic with continued use and can trigger or worsen schizophrenia in vulnerable individuals.

Synthetic Delta-9-THC (dronabinol) is approved for chemotherapy-induced nausea and appetite stimulation, and a Delta-9-THC:CBD formulation is approved in some countries for chronic pain and MS-related spasticity (efficacy in MS largely based on patient report); there are currently no FDA-approved medications specifically for CUD.
harrison.pathophysiology: Delta-9-THC is mainly a partial agonist at G protein-coupled cannabinoid receptors CB1R and CB2R, with euphorigenic effects mediated through CB1Rs on excitatory glutamatergic and inhibitory GABAergic interneurons and glial cells in brain regions processing stress, mood, and reward. These receptors are effectors of the endocannabinoid system (ECS), physiologically driven by endogenous ligands 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG, a full agonist) and anandamide (a partial agonist) that are synthesized and degraded on demand to give temporally and regionally precise modulation. Exogenous cannabinoids, defined by dose and duration rather than this 'just-in-time' synaptic signaling, disrupt ECS neuroregulation. Reward is thought to be mediated by modulation of glutamatergic and GABAergic activity in the ventral tegmental area, from which dopaminergic neurons project to the nucleus accumbens where rewarding experiences are reinforced; anxiolytic effects are mediated via the amygdala. Regular use is associated with broad but reversible reduction in cannabinoid receptor density (recovering by ~28 days of abstinence). Perturbation of ECS signaling during early fetal development can affect neuronal development, migration, and connectivity.

harrison.prognosis: Most acute psychotic episodes are transient, but regular use can render them chronic, and cannabis may trigger or worsen schizophrenia in vulnerable individuals; adolescent and higher-frequency, higher-potency use carries the strongest associations with later psychotic disorder. Receptor downregulation is largely reversible, recovering toward control levels within about 28 days of abstinence. Withdrawal generally resolves within roughly 2 weeks, although insomnia may persist and promote relapse. Earlier age of initiation, higher use frequency, and higher-THC products increase the risk of developing CUD and of progression to other substance use disorders. Adolescent use has been associated with lower grades, lower IQ, and higher school dropout, though causation is not established.
pitfalls: Assuming a plasma Delta-9-THC level reliably reflects impairment; tolerance breaks this correlation and complicates impaired-driving assessment.
Underestimating edible dosing: delayed and variable onset (amplified by fatty meals increasing bioavailability 200-400%) leads naive users to redose and overdose.
Overstating the clinical role of minor cannabinoids (e.g., CBD) or terpenes at the concentrations found in marijuana, where evidence of relevance is limited and largely unproven.
Trusting product potency labels, which testing has shown to be frequently inflated.
Perceiving intoxicating hemp-derived products (e.g., Delta-8-THC and others) as safe or 'legal'; some such products can be considerably more potent than Delta-9-THC.
Overlooking EVALI risk historically tied to vitamin E acetate diluent rather than cannabis itself.
harrison.severityClassification: Cannabis use disorder is diagnosed and graded by DSM-5 criteria (problematic use pattern causing clinically significant impairment or distress), with features including craving, tolerance, a withdrawal syndrome, and failure to fulfill role obligations from recurrent use and drug seeking.
management: Deliver psychosocial treatment as the mainstay, using motivational interviewing, cognitive behavioural therapy and contingency management
Recognise that no pharmacotherapy is firmly established, so drug treatment is not first-line
Manage the withdrawal syndrome supportively, addressing irritability, anxiety, sleep disturbance and reduced appetite
Treat acute intoxication or cannabis-induced psychosis with a benzodiazepine and, where needed, an antipsychotic
Screen for and treat comorbid psychiatric illness, particularly psychosis, depression and suicidality
Screen for co-use of alcohol, nicotine and other substances
Advise harm reduction by lowering potency and frequency, and counsel on risks in pregnancy given the association with lower birth weight and preterm delivery
